title: GAMP 5 Software Categories — Determining Validation Effort
summary: GAMP 5 (Good Automated Manufacturing Practice, 2nd Edition 2022) classifies software into categories that determine the level of validation effort required. The category is based on how configurable/customizable the software is, not its intended use.

Category 1 — Infrastructure Software.description: Operating systems, database engines, middleware, network management tools, antivirus, backup tools
Category 1 — Infrastructure Software.validation_approach: Verify installation, configure per requirements, document version. Qualification focus on infrastructure readiness.
Category 1 — Infrastructure Software.effort: Low — installation verification and configuration documentation

Category 3 — Non-Configured Products (CO.description: Commercial off-the-shelf software used as-is without configuration of business processes. Vendor develops and tests per their SDLC.
Category 3 — Non-Configured Products (CO.validation_approach: Verify installation, confirm vendor qualification, document intended use and user acceptance testing. Leverage vendor testing documentation.
Category 3 — Non-Configured Products (CO.effort: Low to Medium — vendor assessment + user acceptance testing

Category 4 — Configured Products.description: Software products that are configured (not custom-coded) to meet business requirements. The vendor provides the platform; the implementer configures workflows, rules, fields, and processes.
Category 4 — Configured Products.validation_approach: Full validation lifecycle: URS, FS, configuration specification, IQ/OQ/PQ. Focus testing on configured functionality. Leverage vendor's platform validation for core framework.
Category 4 — Configured Products.effort: Medium to High — the bulk of pharma system validation falls here

Category 5 — Custom Applications.description: Bespoke software developed to meet specific requirements. May include custom Apex code on Salesforce, custom integrations, or standalone applications.
Category 5 — Custom Applications.validation_approach: Full SDLC validation: requirements, design, code review, unit testing, integration testing, IQ/OQ/PQ. Source code review and static analysis recommended.
Category 5 — Custom Applications.effort: High — full development lifecycle validation required

note_on_category_2: GAMP 5 Second Edition removed Category 2 (Firmware). Firmware is now treated as infrastructure software (Category 1) unless it is configurable (Category 4) or custom (Category 5).
gotcha: A Salesforce implementation is typically Category 4 (configured), but any Apex custom code elevates those components to Category 5. Most real-world implementations are a MIX of Category 4 and 5.

title: CSV vs CSA — The Industry Shift from Computer System Validation to Computer Software Assurance
summary: The pharmaceutical industry is transitioning from traditional CSV (Computer System Validation) — heavy on scripted testing and documentation — to CSA (Computer Software Assurance), a risk-based approach that focuses testing effort where patient safety and data integrity risk is highest.

csv_traditional.approach: Comprehensive scripted testing of all functionality with detailed test scripts, expected results, and formal protocols. Heavy documentation including Validation Plan, URS, FS, DS, IQ, OQ, PQ, traceability matrices, and Validation Summary Report.
strengths: Accepted by all major regulatory agencies
weaknesses: Extremely documentation-heavy — validation documents can exceed the system documentation itself
Scripted testing often tests the script, not the system
Focus on documentation compliance rather than actual quality assurance
Slow and expensive — delays system deployments
Does not scale well for agile/cloud/SaaS delivery models

csa_modern.fda_guidance: Draft Guidance: Computer Software Assurance for Production and Quality System Software (September 2022)
csa_modern.approach: Risk-based assurance that focuses critical thinking and testing effort on GxP-critical functions. Uses a tiered testing approach: scripted testing for high-risk functions, unscripted (exploratory/ad-hoc) testing for medium-risk functions, and configuration verification for low-risk functions.
key_principles: Assurance activities should be commensurate with risk to patient safety, product quality, and data integrity
Critical thinking over rote documentation — understand WHY a test matters
Unscripted testing (exploratory, error guessing, ad hoc) is ACCEPTABLE for non-critical functions
Vendor testing can be leveraged more extensively — no need to re-test what the vendor already validated
Focus on 'intended use' — validate the system for how it will actually be used, not every possible function
Continuous assurance — ongoing monitoring replaces periodic formal re-validation

risk_tiers.High Risk (Scripted Testing Required): Functions where failure directly impacts patient safety, product quality, or regulatory decision-making. Examples: sample tracking lot traceability, adverse event reporting, batch release decisions, electronic signatures on GxP records
risk_tiers.Medium Risk (Unscripted Testing Acceptab: Functions that support GxP processes but whose failure has detectable, correctable impact. Examples: reporting and analytics, scheduling, territory management
risk_tiers.Low Risk (Verification Only): Functions that do not impact product quality or patient safety. Examples: UI preferences, non-GxP reporting, administrative configuration

adoption_status: CSA is increasingly accepted. FDA published draft guidance in 2022. ISPE GAMP 5 Second Edition (2022) incorporates CSA principles. Many large pharma companies are adopting CSA or hybrid CSV/CSA approaches. However, EU regulators (especially MHRA, ANSM, BfArM) still expect traditional CSV documentation for GMP systems. Japan (PMDA) currently expects traditional CSV.
recommendation: For global implementations, use a hybrid approach: CSA risk assessment to determine testing depth, but maintain CSV-style documentation for GxP-critical functions to satisfy all regulatory expectations. This gives you CSA's efficiency for low/medium-risk functions while maintaining CSV's documentation rigor where regulators expect it.

title: IQ/OQ/PQ — The Qualification Lifecycle
summary: The three-stage qualification process that validates a computerized system from installation through real-world performance. Derived from equipment qualification in pharmaceutical manufacturing and adapted for computerized systems.

IQ — Installation Qualification.purpose: Verify that the system/software is installed correctly per specifications in the defined environment
activities: Verify software version matches approved version
Confirm hardware/infrastructure meets specifications (servers, network, storage)
Validate environment configuration (production, staging, sandbox)
Verify database installation and configuration
Confirm integration endpoints and connectivity
Verify security configuration (SSL/TLS, encryption, authentication)
Document installed components and versions
Verify backup and recovery mechanisms are in place
IQ — Installation Qualification.for_cloud_saas: For SaaS platforms like Salesforce, IQ focuses on tenant configuration: org settings, connected apps, SSO integration, data storage location, and platform version. The vendor handles infrastructure IQ.

OQ — Operational Qualification.purpose: Verify that the system operates as intended within specified operating ranges — test that configured functionality works correctly
activities: Execute functional test scripts for all GxP-critical workflows
Test business rules and validation rules
Verify access controls and permission enforcement
Test audit trail generation and immutability
Verify electronic signature capture, manifestation, and linking
Test data integrity during create/read/update/delete operations
Verify reporting accuracy
Test integration data flows between systems
Boundary and negative testing for critical fields
Test error handling and system behavior under error conditions
OQ — Operational Qualification.for_cloud_saas: OQ is the heaviest phase for SaaS implementations. Focus on configured workflows, custom code (Apex, LWC), validation rules, approval processes, and integrations. Leverage platform vendor's validation for core framework functionality.

PQ — Performance Qualification.purpose: Verify that the system performs consistently and reliably under real-world conditions with actual users and production-like data
activities: End-to-end business process testing with production-representative data
Concurrent user testing at expected load levels
Mobile device testing (offline/online sync, different devices/OS versions)
Performance testing (response times, throughput)
Disaster recovery testing
User acceptance testing (UAT) with trained business users
Verify reporting with production-scale data volumes
Test backup/restore procedures
PQ — Performance Qualification.for_cloud_saas: PQ for SaaS includes testing mobile offline/online workflows, sync reliability under real network conditions, cross-device compatibility, and performance with expected data volumes. Include real-device testing — emulators are insufficient for PQ sign-off.
PQ — Performance Qualification.deliverable: PQ Protocol, PQ Report, and UAT Sign-off

gotcha: IQ/OQ/PQ are NOT always sequential for SaaS systems. Many organizations combine IQ+OQ into a single qualification protocol for cloud systems where the vendor manages infrastructure. The key is that all three qualification purposes are addressed, not that they are separate documents.

title: Risk Assessment Methods for System Validation
summary: Risk assessment is the foundation of both CSV and CSA approaches. It determines which system functions require the most validation effort. Multiple methods can be used; GAMP 5 recommends a risk-based approach throughout the lifecycle.

FMEA — Failure Mode and Effects Analysis.description: Systematic identification of potential failure modes, their causes, and effects. Assigns severity, occurrence, and detectability scores to calculate a Risk Priority Number (RPN).
FMEA — Failure Mode and Effects Analysis.when_to_use: Primary method for detailed risk assessment of individual system functions. Best for systems with clearly defined functions and failure modes.

Initial Risk Assessment (IRA).description: High-level risk assessment performed early in the validation lifecycle to classify the overall system and its major components. Determines GAMP category, GxP impact, and validation scope.
outputs: High-level risk classification of major functions
Initial Risk Assessment (IRA).when_to_use: First step in any validation project. Determines the overall approach and effort level.

Functional Risk Assessment (FRA).description: Detailed risk assessment of each system function/feature to determine testing depth. Maps each function to its GxP impact and assigns a risk classification.

risk_classifications.GxP Critical (High): Direct impact on patient safety, product quality, or data integrity. Requires full scripted testing with documented evidence.
risk_classifications.GxP Relevant (Medium): Supports GxP processes but failure is detectable and correctable. Unscripted testing acceptable under CSA; scripted under traditional CSV.
risk_classifications.Non-GxP (Low): No impact on GxP data or processes. Configuration verification only.

Functional Risk Assessment (FRA).when_to_use: After IRA, during validation planning. Produces the risk-based testing matrix that drives all subsequent qualification activities.

gotcha: Risk assessment must be performed BEFORE writing test protocols, not after. Teams that write tests first and then map them to risks are doing it backwards — the risk assessment should drive the testing strategy, not justify pre-existing tests.

title: Vendor Assessment and Qualification for SaaS/Cloud Systems
summary: For configured products (GAMP Category 4), a significant portion of the validation risk shifts to the vendor. Proper vendor assessment allows organizations to leverage vendor testing and reduce redundant validation effort.
vendor_assessment_scope: Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) — does the vendor follow a formal, documented SDLC?
Change management — how are releases managed, tested, and deployed?
Quality management system — ISO 9001, SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 certifications
Security practices — penetration testing, vulnerability management, incident response
Data center qualifications — physical security, redundancy, backup, disaster recovery
Release management — how are customers notified of changes? Can changes be controlled/deferred?
Audit trail capabilities — native audit trail implementation, immutability guarantees
Data integrity controls — encryption at rest and in transit, backup integrity
Regulatory experience — does the vendor understand GxP requirements?
Previous audit findings — request vendor audit results or SOC reports

vendor_audit_types.Paper-based audit (questionnaire): Minimum requirement. Send vendor qualification questionnaire and review responses.
vendor_audit_types.Remote audit: Virtual walkthrough of SDLC, change management, security, and QMS with vendor quality team.
vendor_audit_types.On-site audit: Physical audit of vendor facilities, development processes, and data centers. Required by some companies for critical GxP systems.
vendor_audit_types.Third-party audit reliance: Accept vendor's SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, or third-party GxP audit reports in lieu of direct audit.

for_salesforce_specifically: Salesforce publishes Trust & Compliance documentation at trust.salesforce.com
SOC 2 Type II reports available under NDA
FedRAMP authorized (relevant for US government life sciences)
Salesforce Shield provides additional audit trail and encryption capabilities
Field History Tracking limitations (20 fields, 18-24 months retention) are a known Part 11 gap
Setup Audit Trail retention is 180 days — insufficient for most GxP retention requirements
Salesforce does NOT provide a Part 11 compliance certification — that responsibility is on the customer/implementer

title: Validation Lifecycle for SaaS/Cloud Platforms
summary: The validation lifecycle for cloud/SaaS platforms differs from traditional on-premise systems because the vendor manages infrastructure, releases updates on a fixed schedule, and customers cannot control platform changes. This requires a continuous validation approach.

key_activities: Map business requirements to system configuration
Classify each function by GxP impact
Assess vendor releases for GxP impact
Validate data migration to new system or archive

saas_specific_considerations: Vendor releases happen on a fixed schedule (e.g., Salesforce 3x/year) — you MUST have a release assessment process
Sandbox refresh strategy is critical for testing — align refresh timing with vendor releases
Multi-tenant architecture means you cannot prevent platform upgrades — plan for continuous validation
APIs and integrations may change between releases — include integration regression testing
Feature flags allow gradual rollout — leverage this for phased validation of new features
